summary: Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV caching recommendations to reduce per-token cost while meeting TideBank latency SLOs. topics: Prefix / KV cache design and hit-rate assumptions

transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining - I'm Maya, AE on the Optimize team, with Jon our SE. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Lena (TideBank): Hi, Lena here.
[00:14] Derek: Derek Shaw.
[00:15] Priya: Priya, security.
[00:17] Sam: Sam.
[00:18] Maya: Awesome. Today we'll walk through batching and the prefix / KV cache recommendations, and run through a simple cost model for your chat workload. We'll keep it pragmatic. Jon, want to kick us off with high level?
[00:27] Jon (Redwood SE): Yeah, thanks. So first quick context from TideBank - we saw in the notes you have a mix of short customer-support prompts and longer context retrieval flows where you append a 4k token. Typical p50/p95 latency targets?
[00:39] Lena: We're aiming p95 under 600 ms for web chat, but some longer retrievals can tolerate up to 2s. Cost is a big factor - we're trying to keep inference spend predictable.
[00:51] Jon: Got it. So two levers we lean on: batching to improve throughput for short requests, and prefix/KV cache to avoid reprocessing cold context for the longer ones.
[01:05] Maya: We'll show some numbers from our cost model - rough ballpark - then adapt to your traffic shape.
[01:12] Speaker 1: Quick question - dedicated GPUs vs hosted? We have compliance constraints so maybe dedicated.
[01:17] Maya: Good flag. We'll show both scenarios; dedicated gives predictable throughput and can be more cost-effective at scale, hosted is easier to start. Also private deployment options if you need VPC.
[01:29] Jon: Slide over to batching: at a high level, continuous batching groups concurrent requests to increase token-parallel utilization. For short 50-150 token responses, batching reduces per-token compute overhead.
[01:45] Lena: Do you recommend fixed-size batching or dynamic?
[01:48] Jon: We recommend adaptive batching for varied traffic. For predictable spikes you can set max batch size and latency SLO. Adaptive lets the runtime build batches up to your latency threshold.
[01:58] [Transcription note: 'adaptive' sometimes heard as 'adoptive']
[02:02] Jon: Example: with a 100ms batch wait and average concurrency of 12, you get ~3-4x token throughput. But there's tradeoff with tail latency.
[02:12] Derek: How do we simulate our traffic for that?
[02:15] Jon: We usually replay a few hours of staging traffic into our bench harness; I can run a 1k request sample to show batching benefit. That's one of the action items.
[02:25] Maya: Now KV / prefix cache. For your retrieval flows where the same doc is appended frequently, a prefix KV cache can store the key-value past key/values so you skip re-encoding large context repeatedly.
[02:37] Sam: Is that the same as 'context caching' - we call it local doc cache.
[02:40] Jon: Similar, but with LLM-serving specifics: we cache KV pairs from the transformer so subsequent calls reuse the cached KV states and only compute the new tokens. Big cost win if hit-rate is high.
[02:50] [00:03] Maya: (small interruption) Also note eviction policy matters - LRU vs TTL depending on doc churn.
[02:59] Priya: Security question - if we cache KV from customer data, is that considered storage of PII? How is it encrypted and auditable?
[03:06] Jon: Great question. On dedicated/private we can encrypt KV at rest with KMS or HSM and restrict access via RBAC. We also log access - audit logs are configurable. On hosted, we provide encryption and audit options too; we'll send SOC2/ISO docs.
[03:19] Priya: Okay please send that.
[03:22] Maya: Will do. Now cost model: rough math. Say baseline per-token cost on hosted for your model variant is $0.00004/token. With batching and a 50% KV hit-rate you can reduce effective per-req cost by ~30-45% depending on sequence lengths.
[03:41] Lena: Can you show a concrete example with our numbers?
[03:44] Jon: Sure. If your average request is 300 prompt tokens + 400 generation tokens, and 30% of calls hit KV cache for the 300 prompt tokens, you only pay full compute on the 70% non-hit prompts. With batching improving throughput, the per-token CPU/GPU amortization drops too.
[04:04] Sam: What about memory footprint for KV? We have lots of small docs.
[04:07] Jon: We size the cache based on expected resident keys; we recommend shard-local KV stores with eviction and compaction. For thousands of docs it's fine; for millions we'd recommend an external key-value store with warmed nodes.
[04:20] [Transcription quirk: 'shard' became 'shardish' in audio]
[04:24] Derek: How does autoscaling interact? If we scale out many GPUs, does cache warm start slow us down?
[04:29] Jon: Warm start is a factor. We use a mix: soft warm (replicate hot keys) and on-demand population. For dedicated pools you can reserve capacity and pre-warm common keys. There's a time vs cost tradeoff.
[04:41] Maya: I'll share a chart in the spreadsheet showing warm-start cost vs reserved capacity.
[04:45] Lena: About hit-rate assumptions - what is realistic?
[04:48] Jon: For customer-support with repetitive prompts, 40-60% is doable. For doc search flows where many queries pull from same doc, hit-rate can be >70%. We used conservative 30-40% in the example.
[04:59] Sam: If a doc changes, do we invalidate the KV automatically?
[05:02] Jon: You can invalidate by key on update; we'd recommend versioned keys so you get deterministic invalidation.
[05:09] Maya: Switching to dedicated vs hosted cost table: dedicated gives lower per-token cost at higher commits. We'll send pricing tiers. Example: dedicated with 8xA100-equivalent has a 25% lower per-token compared to hosted in our sample, but requires commit.
[05:26] Derek: For compliance, we need VPC and KMS support - are those available on dedicated?
[05:30] Maya: Yes, dedicated and private both support VPC, customer-managed keys, and audit logs. We'll attach our compliance pack.
[05:38] Priya: Also need SAML SSO and RBAC.
[05:40] Jon: Supported - SAML, SCIM for user provisioning, RBAC roles for who can view logs.
[05:47] [00:02] Lena: Can we get a sample run showing p95 latency with and without batching?
[05:50] Jon: Yep - that's the 1k request bench. I'll run with your staging traffic sample and show p50/p95 numbers plus cost delta.
[05:58] Sam: One more: do you do quantization recommendations? We care about quality.
[06:02] Maya: Redwood Optimize includes quantization profiles. We recommend mixed precision or 4-bit where quality holds; our eval harness can run your prompts to validate.
[06:11] Jon: We typically run an A/B on quality metrics before recommending 4-bit.
[06:15] [Transcription artifact: 'A/B' as 'a dash B']
[06:18] Derek: Any immediate blockers for a pilot?
[06:21] Maya: Access to a few hours of staging traffic and a contact for infra to enable benchmark runs. Also decision on dedicated vs hosted.
[06:29] Derek: We can share a day of anonymized traffic and a TB staging token.
[06:33] Priya: We'll need to review the SOC2 docs first before granting any sample data.
[06:38] Maya: Totally - we'll get those over (action).
[06:41] [00:01] Jon: Quick demo - live dashboard screenshot (screen share). Showing per-route token breakdown, batching windows, KV-hit heatmap.
[06:52] Lena: The KV-hit heatmap is helpful - can you filter by tenant?
[06:55] Jon: Yes, per-tenant and per-model. You can also set alerts on hit-rate regressions.
[07:02] Maya: Recap / next steps: we'll send pricing and cost model spreadsheet, Jon will run the benchmark, Priya will review the compliance pack, Derek will provide staging traffic sample. We'll schedule the KV tuning deep dive.
[07:16] Lena: Sounds good.
[07:18] Maya: Any other questions?
[07:20] Priya: No, just timeline items.
[07:22] Maya: Great - thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with the artifacts.
[07:27] [End of recording - approximate 45m total]
